title: Steel Framing Product Submittal Checklist: What to Verify Before Approval
description: Use this steel framing product submittal checklist to verify studs, tracks, drawings, code requirements, accessories, and delivery details before approval.
html:
A complete steel framing product submittal should do more than identify a manufacturer. It should show that the proposed steel studs, tracks, channels, clips, accessories, drawings, and supporting documents match the project specifications, design intent, applicable code requirements, and procurement needs. The goal is a traceable package that lets the reviewer confirm what is being supplied and where it belongs.

This checklist is a practical review workflow, not an official Ontario standard or a replacement for project-specific engineering. Product data comes from the manufacturer, while design calculations, approvals, and responsibility for the completed assembly remain with the appropriate project professionals.

Quick summary

  • Start with the project drawings, specifications, schedules, and design criteria before selecting products.
  • Identify every component by product family, profile, dimensions, gauge or thickness, material, and intended use.
  • Separate product data from shop drawings, load tables, and project-specific calculations.
  • Coordinate tracks, bridging, clips, deflection components, resilient channel, trims, fasteners, and adjacent work.
  • Record deviations, confirm current code and specification requirements, and check quantities and delivery details before submission.

What a Complete Steel Framing Submittal Should Prove

The reviewer should be able to follow a clear chain from the project requirement to the proposed product and its supporting documentation. For example, a wall shown as non-load-bearing interior framing should identify the relevant light gauge steel studs, compatible track, spacing or installation requirements where specified, and details needed to coordinate openings and adjacent construction.

A load-bearing or exterior assembly may require a different level of technical information. The package may need heavier framing members, load tables, design criteria, deflection information, wind-related performance data, connection details, or project-specific calculations. Do not treat a general product brochure as proof that a particular configuration satisfies every structural condition.

For a useful comparison of light gauge and heavy gauge applications, review the differences between light gauge and heavy gauge metal stud framing systems. The selection still needs to be checked against the actual drawings and specifications.

Steel Framing Product Submittal Checklist

1. Cover Sheet and Project Identification

Make the package easy to identify and review. Include:

  • Project name, address, and building or area designation.
  • Submittal number, date, revision, and resubmittal status.
  • Submitting contractor, distributor, manufacturer, and contact information.
  • Drawing numbers, specification sections, addenda, and other documents covered.
  • The framing scope, such as interior partitions, shaftwall, exterior framing, acoustic assemblies, or finishing sections.
  • A list of substitutions, deviations, exclusions, and unresolved items.
  • A statement identifying documents that require design-professional review.

If the package covers several areas, separate the information by assembly or location. This reduces the risk that a product approved for one condition is assumed to apply to another.

2. Product Data for Each Framing Component

Every component should be identifiable without guesswork. For steel studs and metal framing, record the product family, profile, section size, length, gauge or thickness, material information, coating information where applicable, and intended application.

Clarify whether each item is a standard product, custom profile, or project-specific configuration. Dass Metal Products states that its technical resources include product brochures, load tables, standards, and safety documentation. Include the documents that apply to the proposed products rather than attaching an unfiltered catalogue.

For track selection, check how the track relates to the stud profile, wall height, deflection condition, opening, and connection detail. This steel track selection guidance can help organize the questions, but the project drawings and specifications control the final selection.

3. Design, Structural, and Performance Information

First classify the framing condition. Non-load-bearing interior light gauge steel framing, load-bearing stud framing, exterior structural framing, shaftwall framing, and acoustic assemblies should not be reviewed as interchangeable systems.

Depending on the project, the submittal may need:

  • Applicable load tables for the proposed member, span, spacing, and support condition.
  • Design loads, serviceability criteria, or deflection limits identified by the project documents.
  • Wind, axial, lateral, or other performance information relevant to the assembly.
  • Connection and fastening information, including manufacturer-stated limits or conditions.
  • Fire, acoustic, thermal, or other assembly documentation when specifically required.
  • Project-specific calculations or sealed drawings prepared by the responsible design professional.

Manufacturer information can describe a product’s properties, but it does not automatically constitute project engineering or approval. Confirm who is responsible for calculations, stamped documents, design coordination, and final acceptance.

4. Accessories and Interfaces

Incomplete accessory information is a common reason for clarification requests. Review the entire framing interface, not only the primary studs. Depending on the assembly, the package may need compatible standard track, slotted deflection track, deep track, bridging or carrying channel, clips, resilient channel, furring channel, shaftwall components, drywall finishing sections, and other trims.

Include only components required by the project. For each accessory, identify its location, purpose, compatible framing member, connection method, and relationship to adjacent materials.

Clips deserve their own check because they often control how framing connects to structure or accommodates movement. Use this metal framing clips selection checklist to confirm the clip type, framing interface, movement condition, fasteners, and supporting documentation.

5. Shop Drawings, Layouts, and Details

Product data identifies what a component is. Shop drawings and layouts show how the proposed framing is arranged for the project. They may be needed when framing is complex, interfaces with several trades, includes custom profiles, or requires coordinated locations and connections.

Where shop drawings are required, check the relevant:

  • Stud and track locations, sizes, spacing, and orientation.
  • Openings, corners, intersections, control joints, and changes in wall direction.
  • Bridging, carrying channel, clips, bracing, and connection locations.
  • Deflection conditions at the head of wall and other movement interfaces.
  • Door, window, equipment, and service penetrations affecting the framing.
  • Interfaces with structure, drywall, shaftwall, ceilings, insulation, and finishes.
  • Details distinguishing standard installation from project-specific conditions.

Do not imply that a manufacturer automatically engineers or stamps project drawings. Establish whether the contractor, consultant, engineer, architect, or manufacturer is responsible for each document and review stage.

6. Standards, Code, and Specification Review

Compare the submittal directly with the contract documents. Check specified material standards, member sizes, thicknesses, coating requirements, fastening provisions, spacing, deflection requirements, fire or acoustic assembly references, and installation instructions.

For Ontario projects, confirm current requirements with the design team and applicable municipal authority. Ontario identifies the 2024 Building Code Compendium as the current reference listed on its official Building Code page, and the Code is enforced by municipal building officials. See the Ontario Building Code information for the current government reference.

Do not describe this checklist as an Ontario government, CSSBI, or industry-issued form. It is a practical way to organize information that project reviewers commonly need.

Component Verification Table

Use this table as a starting point. The exact information required depends on the project specifications, design, assembly, and authority having jurisdiction.

ComponentVerifyDocumentation and review questions
Steel studsLoad condition, profile, size, length, gauge or thickness, spacing, material, and coatingDoes the member match the wall schedule and design criteria? Are load tables or calculations required?
Standard trackCompatible profile, size, thickness, length, and connection conditionDoes the track match the stud and top and bottom support details?
Slotted deflection trackSlot configuration, dimensions, movement condition, and compatible studIs expected movement documented? Are installation and fastening details coordinated?
Deep trackDepth, profile, thickness, stud compatibility, and intended locationDoes the deeper section address the specified head, base, or interface condition?
Bridging channelSection, spacing, connection method, and purposeIs bridging required for the selected stud and assembly? Are supports and clips shown?
Resilient channelProfile, orientation, spacing, attachment, and adjacent layersDoes installation match the specified acoustic or separation assembly?
Clips and connectorsType, capacity or movement function where applicable, fasteners, and interfacesIs each clip compatible with the framing and supporting structure? Are locations shown?
Drywall finishing sectionsProfile, dimensions, material, corner or edge condition, and finish interfaceDoes the trim suit the board thickness, corner geometry, and specified finish?

Questions to Ask the Steel Framing Manufacturer

Ask focused questions before finalizing the package, especially where the project needs a non-standard size or profile:

  • What product family and profile match the specified application?
  • What gauge or thickness, dimensions, length, material, and coating should appear in the submittal?
  • Is the requested section standard or custom?
  • Which brochures, standards, load tables, safety documents, or installation information apply?
  • Are compatible tracks, channels, clips, trims, or connectors available?
  • What information is needed to evaluate a custom profile or project-specific request?
  • Are minimum order, packaging, length, quantity, or handling considerations relevant to the schedule?
  • Which information can the manufacturer provide, and which calculations or approvals must come from the project design team?

When requesting help, provide the project location, framing use, drawings or sketches, required dimensions, gauge or thickness if known, quantities, lengths, performance criteria, delivery destination, and submission deadline. Clear input helps distinguish a product inquiry from a design request.

Procurement and Delivery Details to Confirm

A technically correct submittal can still create procurement problems if approved information does not match the order. Confirm approved product descriptions, quantities, lengths, packaging requirements, sequencing, delivery address, site access limitations, unloading arrangements, and required shipping documents.

Keep procurement aligned with the approved revision. If a product, gauge, profile, or quantity changes after review, document the change and determine whether a revised submittal is needed. Dass Metal Products is based in Vaughan, Ontario, and states that it serves projects across Ontario, Canada, and the United States, including cross-border delivery. Availability and timing should still be confirmed for the specific project.

Final Pre-Submission Review

  • Project name, submittal number, revision, and specification references are correct.
  • Every proposed stud, track, channel, clip, trim, and accessory has a clear product description.
  • Profiles, dimensions, lengths, gauges or thicknesses, materials, and coatings match the project documents.
  • Light gauge, heavy gauge, load-bearing, exterior, deflection, acoustic, and finishing applications are correctly separated.
  • Product data, applicable load tables, shop drawings, layouts, and calculations are included or clearly assigned.
  • Openings, bridging, clips, connections, deflection conditions, and adjacent-trade interfaces are coordinated.
  • Deviations, substitutions, exclusions, and unresolved questions are plainly marked.
  • Applicable code, standards, municipal review expectations, and project specifications have been checked.
  • Design, engineering, and approval responsibilities are understood.
  • Quantities, lengths, packaging, delivery location, and required documentation align with procurement needs.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between steel framing product data and shop drawings?

Product data describes a component, including its profile, dimensions, material, gauge or thickness, and general application. Shop drawings show how components are arranged for a particular project, including locations, openings, connections, interfaces, and details. A project may require one or both.

When does a steel framing submittal need load tables or project-specific calculations?

Load tables or calculations may be relevant when framing carries load, resists wind or other forces, spans a specified distance, supports an assembly, or must meet a defined deflection criterion. The project documents and responsible design professional determine what is required. A general product sheet is not a project-specific calculation.

Should every steel framing accessory be included?

Include every accessory required to understand, install, and review the proposed assembly, but do not add unrelated catalogue products. Tracks, bridging, clips, deflection components, resilient channel, furring channel, and finishing trims should be included when the project uses them or when they affect the proposed interface.

What should an Ontario contractor verify before submitting steel framing products?

Verify the contract specifications, drawings, referenced standards, current Building Code requirements, municipal review expectations, and project-specific fire, acoustic, structural, or deflection criteria. Ontario’s Building Code is enforced by municipal building officials, so confirm questions with the design team and applicable authority.

What information should I provide when requesting a custom steel framing profile?

Provide the intended use, sketches or drawings, required geometry, dimensions, gauge or thickness, material and coating requirements, lengths, quantities, performance criteria, interfaces, delivery location, and submission deadline. Identify whether the request concerns product information, fabrication, engineering input, or a project submittal document.

Conclusion

The strongest steel framing product submittal is traceable. It connects each project requirement to a clearly identified product, relevant technical document, coordinated drawing or detail, and person responsible for design review or approval. It also distinguishes standard manufacturer information from project-specific engineering and calculations.

Use this checklist before submission, then resolve gaps in dimensions, gauge, accessories, connections, code review, documentation, and delivery planning.
